q: Two consumers share this queue. Under load, a consumer sometimes returns a garbage item and `count` jumps to a huge number. Which bug is this?
options: `if` instead of `while`: after waking, another consumer may already have taken the item (or the wakeup was spurious), so it pops from an empty queue
`pthread_cond_wait` doesn't release the mutex, so the producer can't push
explain: A wakeup only means "go and look". Between the producer's signal and this thread re-acquiring the lock, a second consumer can take the item (a stolen wakeup), and POSIX also allows spurious wakeups. With `if`, the thread pops from an empty ring and `count--` wraps around. `while` re-checks the condition. `volatile` is irrelevant because the mutex already orders the memory, `cond_wait` *does* release the mutex atomically, and the modulo is fine.

q: `bq_close()` sets `closed = true` and calls `pthread_cond_signal(&not_empty)` once. Three consumers are blocked on an empty queue. What happens at shutdown?
options: All three wake up and return -EPIPE
One wakes up and returns -EPIPE. The other two sleep forever, and `pthread_join` on them hangs
None wake up, because a signal is lost if it's sent before closing
The program crashes because `signal` needs the mutex unlocked
explain: `signal` wakes (at least) **one** waiter. When a state change matters to *every* waiter, such as a shutdown flag, you need `pthread_cond_broadcast`. Signalling with or without the mutex held is legal, and the woken thread does see `closed` because the flag was set under the lock.

q: Which statements about `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` on glibc are true?
options: A default `PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER` mutex has priority inheritance turned off
It's the POSIX version of `rtos_mutex_create(true)` from Fundamentals
It boosts the mutex owner to the priority of the highest-priority waiter while the owner holds the lock
explain: PI is opt-in. The default mutex's futex only says locked/unlocked/contended, and the kernel never boosts anyone, which makes contention a bit cheaper. Setting `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` needs no privileges, and it does exactly what the Fundamentals inheritance mutex did: the owner temporarily runs at the highest waiter's priority, so a medium task can't starve it. It doesn't replace a real-time policy, though. Priorities only mean something under SCHED_FIFO/RR, and *that* needs CAP_SYS_NICE or rtprio.

q: You set `SCHED_FIFO` priority 80 on a `pthread_attr_t` and create the thread as root. `pthread_create` returns 0, but `chrt -p` shows the thread running as SCHED_OTHER. Why?
options: You forgot `pthread_attr_setinheritsched(&attr, PTHREAD_EXPLICIT_SCHED)`, so the thread inherited the creator's policy and ignored the attr
The kernel needs PREEMPT_RT for SCHED_FIFO
explain: By default a new thread *inherits* its scheduling from the creating thread (`PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED`), and the policy and priority in the attr are silently ignored. 1–99 is a valid range, SCHED_FIFO works on any mainline kernel (PREEMPT_RT only makes it more deterministic), and RT throttling limits CPU time without changing the policy.
